title: Hud and 'Ad
hook: Hud warns the builders of high towers, and the wind comes (7:65–72)

segments.voice: Yesterday: humbly and in secret. Your line was humbly, in secret. Did you find a quiet moment for one ask? Today surah seven begins a run of prophets, one people at a time. Day four hundred nine.
screen: `HUMBLY AND IN SECRET — HUMBLY, IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Cities race each other for the tallest building, and boast when they win. Glass towers, stone walls, a bigger house, a bigger bank balance, a big following. Building isn't wrong. But sometimes people build not to shelter anyone, only to feel that nothing can touch them. The Qur'an tells of an ancient Arabian people called 'Ad, famous for their strength and their building, and of a man from among them sent to warn them. His name was Hud.
screen: `EVERY AGE HAS ITS TALLEST BUILDING.` → `BUILT TO FEEL UNTOUCHABLE.` → `A PEOPLE CALLED 'AD.`

segments.voice: Surah seven, verse sixty-five, introduces him simply: to 'Ad, their brother Hud. Not a stranger. One of their own. His message is the one Nuh brought just before him: my people, worship Allah, you have no god but Him. He reminds them that Allah made them successors after the people of Nuh and gave them great stature and strength. The chiefs answer that he's a fool and a liar, and they say they will not leave what their fathers worshipped. The story is told in several surahs, and they fill in the picture. In surah twenty-six, Hud asks them: do you build a landmark on every high place, just for show, and fortresses, as if you'll live forever? In surah forty-one, they boast: who is mightier than us in strength? Surah eighty-nine names their city Iram, of the lofty pillars. Then the end. Surah forty-six says they saw a cloud coming toward their valleys and said, this cloud will bring us rain. It wasn't rain. Surah sixty-nine calls it a furious, roaring wind, sent against them for seven nights and eight days, until they lay like the hollow trunks of palm trees. Surah seven says simply that Allah saved Hud and those with him, and cut off the rest. Where were they? Surah forty-six places them at al-Ahqaf, the sand dunes, which commentators set in southern Arabia. More than that, the sources don't say for certain. The lesson doesn't need the map. Towers, pillars, strength: none of it was safety.
screen: `THEIR BROTHER HUD.` · `A LANDMARK ON EVERY HIGH PLACE.` · `A CLOUD THEY THOUGHT WAS RAIN.` · `SEVEN NIGHTS, EIGHT DAYS.` · then, large: `TOWERS AREN'T SAFETY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Ask yourself, honestly: what do I build to feel strong? Savings, a title, a reputation, a body at the gym, the number of people who'd take my side. None of these is bad. Pick one, and hold it in your mind. Then ask: if it were gone tomorrow, what would still hold me up? Stay with whatever answer comes, even if it's quiet. The bell holds the time.
Hud and 'Ad. A prophet sent to his own people, the great builders of ancient Arabia, who trusted their strength until the wind came. Today's word.
Your line: towers aren't safety. Today, when you reach for the thing that makes you feel strong, notice it, and remember the wind. Day four hundred nine.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Hud as a prophet sent to the Arabian people of 'Ad; surah eleven bears his name, and teachers read his story as a warning against trusting strength and wealth instead of God.

fork.setup: you're one of 'Ad, and a dark cloud rolls toward your valley after a long dry spell. what did they say?
options: this cloud will bring us rain.
fork.reveal: they welcomed it as rain. surah 46 says it was the very thing they had asked to hurry: a wind with a painful punishment.

original.note: Arabic: Hud, the prophet sent to 'Ad; surah eleven is named for him.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient people destroyed by a storm.
what it means: a people warned by one of their own, who trusted their towers and strength instead of God.

what a scholar hears: the story is distributed across 7, 11, 26, 41, 46, 69 and 89; the Qur'an calls 'Ad successors after Nuh's people, and Iram 'of the pillars' remains debated as a city, a tribe or both.

notes: All verses paraphrased; no direct quotation.
The outline hook mentions 'high towers'; the script draws that from 26:128–129 (landmarks on high places, strongholds) and 89:7 (Iram of the pillars). Confirm the framing.
Location at al-Ahqaf (46:21), placed by commentators in southern Arabia; the script says more is uncertain. Confirm.
Iram as city or tribe is debated; stated in the trapdoor.
